The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to hold its benchmark interest rate steady. At the press conference that followed, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh disclosed some of his thinking about where the U.S. economy stands, and how that affects monetary policy. But for Fed wonks, the big news may have been Warsh's disclosure of some procedural changes ahead.
Here are five key takeaways:
- No surprises: Markets had been widely expecting the Fed to hold, and it did just that. In explaining its decision, the Federal Open Market Committee emphasized a patient approach, saying, "The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
- Well, one surprise: If there was one eyebrow-raising moment from the afternoon, it was Warsh's disclosure of changes in how the FOMC will meet. In 2027, the committee will still meet eight times, but one of the meetings will not entail a vote on interest rates, or include a post-meeting statement. The "strategy" meetings will increase to two the next year, leaving just six opportunities to adjust rates — outside of emergency meetings.
- OK, two surprises: The FOMC vote to hold policy where it stands was widely expected. Dissent from multiple members also came as no shock. But one of the "no" votes coming from Governor Lisa Cook was a stunner. Governors rarely dissent from rate votes, and Cook hasn't done so at all since taking her seat in 2022. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack also opposed the decision. Both likely will provide statements explaining their votes before the end of the week.
- The AI impact: Warsh took the opportunity to talk about the impact artificial intelligence is having on economic growth, essentially saying that it was just one of several factors driving an expansion that he said was running strong.
- More musical chairs: The September meeting featured a shortened post-meeting news conference — cut from the usual 45 minutes or so down to half an hour, about the time of Wednesday's event. Moreover, reporters have been limited to a single question, a switch from prior practices when media members would take a two-for-one approach. Finally, Warsh has changed the seating in the room, going from a largely arbitrary approach — with representatives of larger outfits up front — to alphabetical order last month. This month featured reverse alphabetical order, keeping the bearers of the microphone on their toes.
What they're saying:
"The Fed is leaning into patience. It seems they prefer to wait for more information on the appropriate level of rates, as uncertainty reigns supreme in light of recent geopolitical developments." —Phil Camporeale, chief investment strategist, JPMorgan Wealth Management.
"The Fed has time on its side ... But the direction of travel remains clear. The Fed is still taking back some of last year's rate cuts, and the two dissents underline that tightening bias. We expect a hike in December and another in early 2027." — Seema Shah, chief global strategist, Principal Asset Management.
"We hesitate to characterize his communication as particularly dovish or hawkish ... The bottom line is that the Fed policy reaction is not a black-and-white, binary thing ... The market has adjusted to Warsh's communication style, but there might be a ways to go before they are fully on the same page." — Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist,

That doesn’t necessarily mean you shouldn’t go out at night: Whether you want to avoid the daytime heat, short winter days are cutting into your schedule, or you simply prefer it, sometimes night time is the right time. It is in your best interest to take any step you can to increase your visibility, though, so you should always wear reflective running gear when you run in twilight or after dark.
Happily for my fellow night-time running enthusiasts and I, there is a growing range of athletic apparel with high-visibility elements to make sure drivers, bikers, and other pedestrians see you. Clothing in fluorescent colors helps, but reflective panels, which light up in the face of car headlights, make your presence well-known and keep you safe on a night run. I’ve picked out the best reflective running gear, including hats, pants, shirts and more.

Once you know what kind of reflective clothing you want, there are a few details you should look at closely.

These institutions benefit from rising interest rates that improve NIMs (net interest margins), digital transformation reducing operational costs, and expanding wealth management services as populations age. Economic downturns also pose risks through potential loan defaults and compressed margins during accommodative monetary policy periods.

Two tech behemoths -- Alphabet (GOOG +1.60%) (GOOGL +1.34%) and Microsoft (MSFT -0.06%) -- reported earnings today. Both showed strong cloud growth, but the market is treating them very differently. Microsoft shares popped after hours while Alphabet stock sank. Why?
I think a big part of the answer is how each plans to pay for the massive outlays both have planned.
Cloud growth accelerated at both companies
Microsoft beat Wall Street's targets with sales up 19%, reaching $92.3 billion. GAAP -- generally accepted accounting principles -- earnings per share (EPS) came in at $4.92. Adjusted EPS was $4.89, above the roughly $4.72 the Street expected. Azure, its cloud platform, grew 48%, reaching $33.17 billion in revenue.
Alphabet's cloud growth was even stronger than Microsoft's: 103% growth for the unit, earning $11.1 billion in operating income on $30.7 billion in sales. Overall, sales jumped 25%, reaching $127.6 billion, slightly missing estimates, while GAAP EPS actually fell from $2.87 to $2.12. Search and YouTube ads also underperformed.
Alphabet's cash flow is the real problem
Some of Alphabet's EPS drop can be explained by an $8.7 billion net loss on equity securities, but even if you remove this -- worth $0.55 per share -- the earnings still came in well below what Wall Street was looking for.
While it's not a great look, I think the real issue the market is reacting to is the company's cash picture. Alphabet spent $51.4 billion on capital expenditures (capex), up from $24.0 billion a year ago. Operating cash flow -- the cash the actual business generated -- was $42.3 billion. That left free cash flow (FCF) -- the money left after paying for its capex investments -- at negative $9.1 billion. That's worse than the negative $5.9 billion the company reported last quarter.
During the quarter, Alphabet raised $28.7 billion through senior unsecured notes and $12.4 billion from selling stock. Long-term debt has grown from $46.5 billion at the end of 2025 to $125.1 billion.
Alphabet said its capex guidance for 2026 holds -- $195 billion to $205 billion -- but said it expects capex in 2027 to "increase significantly."
Microsoft is still paying its own way
Microsoft, on the other hand, is still FCF positive, though like Alphabet, that figure is moving in the wrong direction. The company reported FCF of $18.63 billion, down 27% year over year, after $39.37 billion in cash capital spending. Its broader capex figure, which includes finance leases, was $45.2 billion.
CFO Amy Hood said on July's earnings call that the company expects to stay free-cash-flow positive for its current fiscal year, though capex is expected to expand. On that call, she also said demand for its cloud services was running ahead of supply.
The bottom line
Microsoft at this point has a much healthier cushion in its quarterly cash flow -- more room to keep spending while it waits for those investments to pay off. Alphabet is increasingly asking lenders and shareholders to help cover the bill.
Obviously, the growth is hard to argue with, but I still think the jury is out on whether this bet will pay off for both companies. Costs are climbing, and I'm concerned the math won't pencil out long

The surge in construction of fossil-fueled power plants to run AI data centers is set to undo 15 years’ worth of greenhouse gas reductions from US electricity generation, according to an internal analysis by the Sierra Club.
The US power sector would emit 2.1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide by 2030, after factoring in planned AI projects. That’s 618 million tons more than 2025 levels, by the Sierra Club’s calculations, or about a 42% increase.
A year and a half ago, researchers at the nonprofit environmental group would have estimated that the buildout and its impact would have been a quarter or half of current projections, said Jeremy Fisher, the Sierra Club’s principal advisor for climate and energy. “The numbers continue to sort of boggle our minds,” he said.
Many data center developers are turning to natural gas to meet the immense electricity demand, relying on power sources that are both on and off the grid. The bulk of the expected emissions by 2030 would come from sources that are not directly linked to the grid, often built by tech companies to avoid the long wait for a connection. These could exceed 460 million tons, Fisher said, roughly the same as the annual emissions of Mexico.
Helen Kou, a BloombergNEF analyst, said if there’s significant growth in gas power for new facilities, “you would presume emissions would increase from year to date.”
But how much is a difficult question to answer. There’s so much uncertainty in the projections for power emissions that the lowest and highest estimates differ by more electricity than the combined demand of California and Florida.
The Sierra Club’s estimate of the climate impacts of the data center buildout is higher than others released so far. The wide range of projections is due to questions around how many facilities will actually be built, what technologies they will ultimately use and how much renewable energy capacity comes online over the next few years.
The environmental nonprofit Union of Concerned Scientists in January projected that fossil-fuel-powered electricity for data centers could increase US power-sector emissions by 19% to 29%, or as much as 342 million tons a year by 2035. US and Canadian researchers in June published a journal article projecting a 28% rise in the sector’s emissions.
Other forecasts see US electricity continuing to decarbonize as economically competitive renewables outperform fossil fuels, despite the data center boom. Rhodium Group, a research firm that projects energy use and CO2, finds that in its highest-emission scenario for 2040 that the sector’s greenhouse gas emissions fall 24% below their 2025 level.
If the rush to build AI data centers leads to the upper bounds of the emissions projected by these researchers, it represents a reversal of a two-decade economic and policy trend toward less US power-sector climate pollution.

The top US agency for consumer financial protection is not adequately protecting databases with large volumes of sensitive consumer and business information, potentially exposing them to hackers or theft, a watchdog report said on Oct. 28.
The audit, which found the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s information security program “not effective,” follows nearly two years of upheaval at the agency which the Trump administration last year initially moved to abolish, abruptly closing offices, halting work, canceling contracts and seeking to cut staff en masse.
CFPB representatives did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday but in a written response to the audit, officials said they accepted its recommendations and had made substantial progress in improving conditions after the audit was finished.
According to the Federal Reserve-CFPB Inspector General’s office, the CFPB failed to inventory several actively used datasets, potentially leaving them vulnerable.
The agency also failed to remedy “critical and high-severity” vulnerabilities within a required 30-day period and had outdated or insufficient policies on cybersecurity risk and impact analyzes, the audit found.
The findings followed a separate IG report last month which said the agency was unable to vouch for the security of computer hardware in its former regional offices, which the Trump administration shuttered last year.
In a written response to the audit, Christopher Chilbert, the CFPB’s chief information officer, noted that the agency had not had any major security incidents or breaches involving individuals’ personal information in the government’s last fiscal year and was working on addressing other deficiencies.
“In summary… the Bureau has already done the work of addressing most of the… recommendations and the Bureau will continue to focus” on further improvements, said Chilbert.

A father and son have been charged with running an illegal “chop-shop” in Pennsylvania involving illegal titling and sales of stolen vehicles with counterfeit documents.
Attorney General Dave Sunday said that Jermaine Quinones Sr., 42, and Jermaine Quinones Jr., 18, have each been charged with corrupt organizations, theft by deception, washing vehicle titles, insurance fraud and other crimes.
The pair ran a chop shop throughout 2026, “washing” titles of vehicles that were known to be stolen with vehicle identification numbers (VINs) and other information not belonging to the stolen vehicles, according to officials.
They said many of the vehicles were then sold on Facebook Marketplace and many were new and of high value, including 2026 model Infiniti QX60 ($67,599 value), Acura Integra ($35,950), and two Ford Mustangs ($32,640 and $31,890).
investigators said they identified sales of 12 vehicles with washed paperwork, valued at nearly $500,000 between 2025 and 2026,
The older Quinones was arrested earlier this month at his Allentown home. He was arraigned on the charges and bail was set at $450,000 cash. His son was arrested October 22. At arraignment, bail was set at $100,000. The criminal charges are merely allegations and the father and son are presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty.
The investigation was carried out by the Attorney General’s Insurance Fraud Section, Pennsylvania State Police, and Monroe County Detectives.
“This criminal conduct is harmful in many ways, as it defrauds the Commonwealth’s vehicle titling system and insurance providers, and unsuspecting buyers who are left with ‘dirty’ vehicles,” Attorney General Sunday said. “The vehicle titling and registration system exists to protect consumers and insurance providers, and ensure vehicles on Commonwealth roadways are safe.”

Columbia University has opened the window for individuals impacted by the school’s data breach last year to claim part of a $16.1 million settlement.
The university agreed in September to settle a proposed class action over the incident, with affected individuals eligible for credit monitoring, identity-theft restoration services and cash payments. Claims are due Jan. 21, 2027, according to a notification sent to people affected by the breach.
The settlement stems from a cybersecurity incident first reported by Bloomberg that exposed information belonging to millions of people, including university applicants. The compromised data included Social Security numbers, addresses, demographic information, financial-account details, academic histories and medical information, according to the notification.
Columbia University Hack Affected 870,000 People, Included Some Health Data
The Manhattan-based university tallies roughly 3.1 million individuals affected by the breach, up from last year’s count of about 870,000 individuals, according to information filed with state officials in May. A Columbia official said in August the “data types affected during this incident differed for each individual, so that not every type of data was necessarily affected for every person.”
The university said Friday it had found no evidence the cyber-attack was financially motivated or that the data was sold or distributed on the dark web.
Hacked Columbia University Data Includes Banking Numbers, GPAs
After Columbia discovered the incident in June 2025, hackers continued to strike the university’s Ivy League peers through the end of the year, leaving behind a trail of data breaches.
Hackers Strike Ivy League Schools Already Under Political Pressure
A data breach at the University of Pennsylvania affected 440,000 individuals and another at Dartmouth College affected 99,000 individuals, according to data from the Texas Attorney General. The universities’ reports to state officials indicate the breaches contained Social Security numbers and financial information.

The Connecticut town of East Haven is appealing a federal district court ruling that rejected its claim for insurance coverage for a civil lawsuit and $11 million judgment against it regarding the closure of a local quarry in 2017 for political reasons.
The $11 million was awarded to quarry owners who alleged that the town interfered with their operations through various regulatory measures before eventually shutting it down through a series of cease-and-desist orders in 2017. The quarry owners sought damages in excess of $25 million for actions by the town and its officials they say violated their federal and state constitutional rights.
The town had two different liability insurers, Starr Indemnity and Liability, and Allied World Insurance. Both insurers disclaimed duties to defend and indemnify the town for the quarry owners’ civil case under the terms of their policies.
The town sued to force the insurers to defend and indemnify it for the quarry owners’ lawsuit. In September, the federal district court for Connecticut granted summary judgment to the two insurers. The district court found that neither insurer breached a duty to indemnify or defend. In the case of Starr, the actions taken by the officials that closed the quarry were taken outside of the policy period. In Allied World’s case, an exclusion for claims related to the “lack of due process” barred coverage.
On October 21, the town informed the court it would be appealing that district court decision and the final judgement to the Second Circuit Court of Appeals.
The underlying action brought against the town, former Mayor Joseph Maturo, Jr., a zoning official and the town tax assessor by the quarry was filed in June 2017. The plaintiffs were John Patton, One Barberry Real Estate Holding, LLC and Farm River Rock LLC, who owned and operated a quarry in East Haven.
According to their complaint, the town’s actions included reclassifying portions of the quarry as industrial land and taxing it at a higher rate than previously beginning in October 2015; informing Patton that blasting permits would not be granted in the months preceding the 2015 municipal election; and issuing three cease-and-desist orders between February and May 2017, the last of which instructed the owners to completely shut down their quarry operations.
A federal judge in a bench trial concluded that the town and officials infringed on the quarry owners’ constitutionally protected property right in an arbitrary and irrational manner, in violation of their Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process protections. The judge awarded damages of $9,465,832. The quarry owners moved to alter the judgment and were granted prejudgment interest and attorneys’ fees and costs, bringing the total to $11,000,000.

Anthropic told California Gov. Gavin Newsom that government officials should be able to seek court orders blocking the release of AI models that pose a “serious risk” to the public, according to an October 15 letter that echoed the company’s earlier policy proposals.
Anthropic itself has faced government restrictions on its AI systems. The Trump administration in June ordered Anthropic to immediately restrict foreign access to its cyber-capable Mythos 5 and Fable 5 models, citing national security concerns. The U.S. Commerce Department later lifted the order.
“When a review finds a model poses a serious risk, the government should be able to ask a court to block it,” the letter to Newsom said.
An Anthropic spokesperson confirmed the letter is authentic. The California governor’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Related: Anthropic Filing Reveals Concerns Over Data Center Pushback
Anthropic submitted the recommendations after the governor in September convened a panel of artificial intelligence experts to develop proposals for AI safety requirements.
The company also said it opposes requirements that developers build “kill switches” capable of shutting down entire AI models in the event a company loses control over their actions. Instead, Anthropic supports more targeted interventions, such as disabling a problematic AI agent or cutting off a specific customer’s access to a model, according to the letter, saying they would be more effective.
A bipartisan group of U.S. senators in September were debating legislation that would give the U.S. government the power to block the release of certain AI models that are deemed unsafe, Reuters reported, and companies would be able to challenge that decision in federal court. Congress left for its pre-election break shortly after, and lawmakers have not moved forward on that proposal.
Related: Anthropic Pitches AI Safety Bill to Lawmakers
U.S. House lawmakers in July proposed the “AI Kill Switch Act,” which would give U.S. officials the power to order AI firms to shut down models that put human life or the economy at risk.
Anthropic is preparing for a U.S. initial public offering. The listing would represent one of the most consequential stock market debuts in years, potentially reshaping benchmark indexes, investor flows and the broader narrative driving U.S. equities.
Politico first reported the details of the letter.

The U.S. government isn’t doing enough to fight the surge in cyberscams, and partnerships with the private sector remain fragmented and voluntary, an investigation into the global scam industry led by the Joint Economic Committee of the U.S. Congress has found.

“Transnational criminal organizations run massive compounds that exploit U.S. technology, including AI, to carry out scams against Americans with devastating consequences,” Hassan said in an email. “The scale of this exponentially growing challenge requires Congress, the Administration, and the private sector to all strengthen their efforts.”
The report, which the AP obtained before its release, made clear how hard it is for scam victims to get their money back, despite the quickening pace of seizures announced by a variety of U.S. government agencies.
The FBI told the committee that it returned $336 million to scam victims in 2025.
The Federal Trade Commission reported that it had returned $1.83 billion to fraud victims in fiscal year 2025, but couldn’t determine how much of that money had been lost to overseas scam compounds.
The U.S. Secret Service returned more than $770 million in seized assets to fraud victims in fiscal years 2024 and 2025, but noted the money had come from a range of fraud schemes.
The U.S. State Department said that foreign law enforcement agencies that receive support from the department had seized proceeds “in the low hundreds of millions of dollars,” but told Congress to ask the Departments of Justice, Homeland Security and Treasury for details.

Twenty-one US states and the District of Columbia sued President Donald Trump’s administration on Tuesday over its rollback of reporting requirements established under a 2021 law aimed at combating illicit finance.
The Trump administration in August finalized a rule exempting US companies and individuals from reporting beneficial ownership information to the Treasury Department’s financial crimes unit, rolling back reporting requirements established under the 2021 Corporate Transparency Act.
In their lawsuit, the coalition of mostly Democratic-led states asked a federal court to overturn the rule, which was part of a broader push by the Trump administration to curtail anti-corruption efforts.
“The executive branch cannot repeal a law by rulemaking. That fundamental principle resolves this case,” said the lawsuit filed in the US District Court for the District of Oregon.
The lawsuit said that the Trump administration effectively gutted the 2021 law by exempting more than 99.9% of companies originally required to disclose information about their owners.
The suit was filed against US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the Department of the Treasury and its anti-money laundering Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.
The Treasury Department did not respond to a request for comment.
Bessent had cast the rule when it was made in August as “eliminating a burdensome reporting requirement for millions of law-abiding business owners without compromising our national security.”
The lawsuit also listed the heads of the US Departments of Justice and Homeland Security as defendants.
“The Trump administration has effectively overturned this law by enacting a rule that exempts all domestic companies and US owners of foreign companies from the law’s requirements, allowing the true owners of both foreign and domestic shell companies to remain anonymous,” New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was among the more than 20 state attorneys general who filed the challenge, said in a statement.
US Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee, said in August that rolling back the reporting requirements increased the risks of sanctions evasion, fraud and drug trafficking, as well as sex trafficking and organized criminal activity.
(Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Bill Berkrot)

A catastrophic 2025 Los Angeles firestorm exposed some 7 million people to high levels of airborne lead and other toxic metals released from burning homes and vehicles, according to a new study.
Scientists for the first time were able to quantify in real time the chemical composition of wildfire smoke thanks to a sensor network that went online months before the January 2025 Eaton conflagration that destroyed more than 9,400 buildings, killing 19 people.
Related: Will California’s New Smoke Claims Law Create a Recovery Bottleneck?
As climate change triggers urban firestorms like the inferno in the LA suburb of Altadena, the paper published Wednesday in the journal Science Advances offers the first indication of how the incineration of homes, electronics, cars and infrastructure could affect even people who live far from the burn zone due to wind-blown toxic smoke.
The researchers determined that over a 24-hour period, smoke from the fire contained 80 times the concentration of lead normally found in the atmosphere. Lead is a neurotoxin linked to an array of health effects and is particularly harmful to children. Sensors also detected highly elevated levels of arsenic and other toxins. The smoke plume covered eastern LA and the San Gabriel Valley and affected about 70% of the county’s population.
Nga Lee (Sally) Ng, a co-author of the study and a professor of environmental science and engineering at the California Institute of Technology, said that while chronic exposure to metals like lead is well-studied, the health effects from short-term exposure to highly concentrated airborne toxins remains largely unknown.
“The hope is that with these real-time measurements, we can better understand and characterize the health impacts of these short-term exposures,” she said.
The data on Eaton was collected by a Los Angeles monitoring site that happened to be downwind of the fire. It’s part of the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry Measurement Network (ASCENT) that has established stations across the country. Ng, who is a principal investigator for the National Science Foundation-funded project, said the LA site wasn’t able to collect data on the Palisades fire, which ignited 34 miles away from the Eaton site hours earlier, due to the wind direction.

ASCENT also allowed the researchers to track how the toxic composition of the smoke plume changed over time as the fire burned, according to Haroula Baliaka, the study’s lead author who was a PhD candidate at Caltech at the time. That could help health researchers pinpoint health impacts from urban firestorms.
She said the study results should encourage policymakers to rethink strategies for evacuating residents from urban wildfires, given toxic smoke exposure can occur far from the burn zone. “I can envision that in the future we have these evacuation zones for smoke exposure as well,” said Baliaka. “Unfortunately, this is not a one-time event. It’s a new reality and we need to adapt to it and we need to do it sooner rather than later.”

Missouri passed a law to compensate the wrongfully convicted. Now it doesn’t want to pay.
Two men are seeking $2.4 million for their combined 38 years lost in prison. The attorney general is fighting them in court.
Dale Helmig is seeking compensation for the more than 14 years he spent wrongfully incarcerated in Missouri (Katie Moore/Marshall Project).
After Missouri lawmakers expanded eligibility for wrongfully convicted people to receive compensation last year, Dale Helmig thought he could get nearly $1 million for the more than 14 years he spent in prison. And Darryl Burton hoped to obtain more than $1.5 million for the 24-plus years he was incarcerated.
But today, they are back in the legal system that put them away. The state attorney general is arguing in court that the two men aren’t innocent, setting aside judges’ prior decisions — and that even if they were, the new law isn’t retroactive.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s effort to fight their compensation requests — the first two under the new compensation law — is part of a long history of the office vigorously opposing innocence claims. Under her predecessors, attorneys there have kept people in prison even after a judge has ordered their release and continued to fight cases in the face of overwhelming evidence of innocence.
Peter Joy, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis, said the Attorney General’s Office “has opposed claims of innocence on a very consistent basis, even though there have been times when the local prosecutor’s offices have recognized that the person had a valid claim of innocence.”
That doesn’t necessarily mean they aren’t examining each case on its merits, Joy said. But if they were opposing these without a “good faith basis,” it would be a violation of prosecutors’ ethical obligation to seek justice, he said. A spokesperson for Hanaway declined to comment, citing the pending cases.
When Helmig and Burton were released from prison, only those exonerated through DNA evidence qualified for state compensation — not people like them, whose convictions were overturned based on recantations or other types of newly discovered evidence.
Then, last year, the Missouri legislature expanded eligibility and increased the amount of money exonerees can collect. The measure was approved by Gov. Mike Kehoe.
The law allocates about $65,000 for every year of wrongful incarceration. That amount is paid on an annual basis, not as a lump sum.
In Helmig’s case, a judge in DeKalb County, about an hour north of Kansas City, ruled in 2010 that there was clear and convincing evidence that he was innocent.
Helmig had been convicted in the 1993 murder of his mother, Norma, whose body was found in a river in central Missouri, near where she lived. Burnout among Missouri’s doctors, lawyers and executives rarely announces itself. It shows up as a surgeon in Kansas City who stops sleeping through the night, a litigator in Clayton who adds a second drink most evenings, a hospital administrator in Springfield who snaps at a staff meeting and spends the drive home replaying it. Their work stays excellent. That is exactly the problem.
I am a licensed clinical social worker, and the people I see most often in this situation are not short on money, insurance or information. They are short on one thing: a way to get help that nobody at work will ever hear about.
The research on attorneys makes that point more clearly than anything else I know. The largest study of lawyer mental health, published in the Journal of Addiction Medicine in 2016, screened 12,825 licensed, employed attorneys. When the authors asked why people had not sought help, the two most common answers were not wanting others to find out and concerns about privacy or confidentiality. Among attorneys who had been in treatment, about half named the first reason.
That finding has held up. A 2026 research paper by my firm, CEREVITY, works through the decade of studies that followed and notes that the headline numbers vary with the method used. The fear of exposure is the one finding that shows up every time someone asks the question, in attorneys and in law students alike.
Doctors and senior executives carry the same calculation. A physician wonders who at the hospital will see the claim. A chief financial officer pictures the board hearing about it. A partner thinks about origination credit and what the firm did the last time someone admitted they were struggling. Each person decides, usually quickly and usually alone, that the safer move is to wait.
Here is what that waiting looks like in practice, in a composite drawn from common patterns rather than any one person. A Kansas City executive notices in January that she is lying awake at 3 a.m. By spring she is canceling lunches and rereading emails four times before sending them. By late summer a colleague asks if she is OK, and she says she is just busy. She finally calls someone in the fall, after a panic attack in a parking garage. European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will step down on Feb. 7 next year, she announced Thursday, formally kicking off a succession race that will be shaped by political bargaining and France's looming fiscal crisis.
Lagarde has led the central bank since July 2019, steering its responses to the Covid-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war and a series of energy price shocks that sent inflation in the European Union above 11% in 2022 and spurred the end of the post-Financial Crisis era of negative interest rates.
Lagarde will depart nearly nine months before her term was due to expire in October 2027, while the process to appoint her successor will begin immediately.
What the ECB is looking for in a successor
Senior ECB figures are already in talks about filling other senior roles, with chief economist Philip Lane and influential executive board member Isabel Schnabel, responsible for market operations, also due to step down next year.
The ECB is institutionally independent, and its Governing Council comprises the six-member Executive Board and the governors of the 21 euro area national central banks.
But appointments to its top jobs are made by the European Council following consultations with the European Parliament and euro area member states, with negotiations generally reflecting political bargaining over national representation and influence.
Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot, who both led their respective central banks for recent stints, are widely regarded as top contenders to replace Lagarde.
De Cos served from 2018 to 2024 and is now general manager of the Bank for International Settlements. Knot was Dutch central bank chief from 2011 until 2025 and is a distinguished visiting fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.
The appointment of a new president is seen as crucial amid market debate over whether the ECB could use one of its intervention mechanisms as France faces a mounting sovereign debt crisis.
France's presidential election, due next year, is injecting further uncertainty as the country's bond yields spike and its spread over euro area benchmark Germany's rises to the highest level since the bloc's Sovereign Debt Crisis of the early 2010s.

A Cole County Circuit Court judge ruled Thursday that a state law allowing charter schools to operate in Boone County is not an unconstitutional special law (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
A 2024 law that allowed charter schools to open in Boone County is not an unconstitutional “special law,” a Cole County judge ruled Thursday.
Columbia Public Schools challenged the statute, arguing that it violated the Missouri Constitution’s prohibition on special laws, which single out localities or people when a general law could apply.
But even though the law singled out Boone County, lawmakers had reasonable grounds for limiting charter school expansion to the county, Circuit Court Judge Emily Fretwell wrote in an 11-page ruling.
Columbia Public Schools has already stated that it plans to appeal the decision.
“While we respect the judicial process, we respectfully disagree with the court’s determination that this provision is not an unconstitutional special law,” the district’s chief communications officer Michelle Baumstark said in a statement.
Previously, charter schools were only permitted in St. Louis and Kansas City school districts, in districts that have lost state accreditation and where a local school district chooses to sponsor a charter school.
“The court only looks for any ‘plausible reason for the classification in question,’” Fretwell wrote, citing a 2011 Missouri Supreme Court case. “Regardless of whether the reasoning is imperfect or speculative.”
The school district had the burden of proving that there is no reasonable explanation for singling out Boone County. Fretwell found “several rational bases” for the law.
She agreed with the Missouri Attorney General’s Office that Boone County had “unique characteristics” that “justify its different treatment compared to all other counties.” Those included the county’s population, large achievement gaps between certain student groups in English and math, its high percentage of college-educated adults and the presence of the University of Missouri-Columbia.
“It is reasonable to believe that the diverse population Mizzou brings to Boone County could uniquely support and benefit from charter schools,” Fretwell wrote.
She also upheld lawmakers’ decision to exempt Boone County from a charter school funding provision. When the legislature expanded charter schools into the county, it excluded the county from a funding provision passed in 2022 that boosted state aid for charter schools elsewhere.
“The General Assembly could reasonably believe that those provisions responded to the specific state of affairs affecting existing charter schools in other jurisdictions,” her decision says. “Because charter schools are new to Boone County, it is uncertain whether those same problems will exist.”
The Missouri Charter Public School Association, which unsuccessfully sought to intervene in the case, said Thursday’s decision “preserves an opportunity for more Missouri families to access tuition-free public schools.”
“We are encouraged by this ruling, which permits greater access to (charter) public schools that fit the needs of students and families in the Boone County area,” said the organization’s executive director Noah Devine.
One charter school, Frontier Charter School, has been approved to open in Boone County. It plans to begin operating in Columbia next year.

Missouri marijuana businesses had reason to celebrate in April when the federal officials moved medical marijuana into a less restrictive category of controlled substances.
The federal order could also set marijuana companies on a path to substantial federal tax savings. For years, federal law has prevented many cannabis businesses from deducting ordinary expenses — including employee salaries, rent and other costs — when calculating their federal taxes.
But months after the change, Missouri businesses still don’t know exactly how to claim those savings, especially if they sell both medical and recreational marijuana.
That uncertainty was a key topic this month on the Missouri Division of Cannabis Regulation’s DCR OutLoud podcast, where leaders of the Missouri Cannabis Trade Association said they’re waiting for federal tax officials to explain how the new rules will work.
“Not only is the cannabis industry here in Missouri one of the most regulated industries, but it’s also one of the most taxed,” said Andrew Mullins, executive director of the association.
The federal tax rule at the center of the debate is known as Section 280E. It generally prevents businesses that sell certain federally prohibited drugs from deducting everyday business expenses. This prohibition results in an effective income tax rate on marijuana businesses of as high as 80%, compared to the standard federal corporate rate of 21%.
Missouri already allows licensed marijuana businesses to deduct those expenses on their state income tax returns, but the federal restriction has remained in place.
The April order moved marijuana regulated under state medical licenses into Schedule III but left recreational marijuana in Schedule I. That leaves businesses that sell both types of cannabis with a difficult question: How much of their spending can they deduct?
“Certainly they’re all very anxious to see if relief is on the way and if we’re going to see that guidance from the IRS that basically directs what they can do…” Mullins said.
In late September, the U.S. Department of the Treasury and Internal Revenue Service listed Section 280E guidance among their priorities for the coming fiscal year, which runs through September 2027. But the list includes more than 100 other tasks.
Amy Moore, director of the Missouri Division of Cannabis Regulation, said the federal order creates a particular challenge for states such as Missouri, where many businesses handle medical and recreational sales under the same license.
“In our state, the difference between medical and just adult-use consumer product really only comes into play at that moment of sale when a particular tax rate is applied,” Moore said on the podcast. “But that [Department of Justice] order seems to be really organized around medical marijuana.”
Drew Lammert, chair of the trade association’s government affairs committee, said businesses may have to make their own decisions about how to divide expenses between medical and recreational sales while they wait for federal guidance.
Lammert is also the co-founder of High Fidelity Brands, where he says medical marijuana sales make up only 10% of the company’s business.
“We are excited, but there’s also those questions of the unknowns,” he said, “and what does that mean for the 90% of adult use sales out there.”

- Nike has announced its newest pinnacle racing shoe, the Apex
- It features a redesigned midsole with stacked Zoom Air units
- The new marathon racing model will be released on January 7
The super shoe frenzy just got even more intense: Nike recently announced the Apex, the brand’s latest elite marathon racer. The Apex won’t go on sale until January 7, 2027, but pros are already wearing it—and it’s already on the podium. Here’s what you need to know about this soon-to-be-released super shoe.
Specs
From a distance, the Apex follows the same general design as the Alphafly models before it: an airy mesh upper over a thick foam midsole with a carbon fiber plate and Zoom Air units in the forefoot. But the Apex has some major updates compared to its forebears. The most obvious: This shoe features four Zoom Air units, arranged in two sets stacked on top of each other, in the forefoot (the Alphafly 4 has only two such units). The ZoomX LT foam, a revised PEBA-based material also used in the Alphafly 4, returns in the Apex, but Nike tweaked the carbon fiber plate design to guide your foot forward onto the Zoom Air units for maximum responsiveness and propulsion. All that adds up to a shoe that weighs a feathery 5.9 ounces in men’s size 10.
The other big change? The Apex is a zero-drop shoe, measuring an even 40mm across at both the heel and forefoot. No other super shoe on the market has a zero-drop platform; even Altra, a brand famous for its zero-drop models, gave its top-tier racer a 4mm drop. Nike claims the flat footbed provides a more balanced ride and lets the brand pack more cushioning into the Apex without breaking the World Athletics 40mm stack height limit.
Super shoes aren’t designed for durability, but Nike definitely wants you to save the Apex for race day only. In the shoe’s official press release, the brand notes it’s designed “to serve runners for at least 100 kilometers.” That means you can expect to cover about 62 miles in these kicks before they start to wear out.
What It Means
As usual, Nike makes bold claims about its new design, but the stats for the Apex are particularly impressive. Nike reports the new shoe generates up to 40% more energy return than the Alphafly 3 (the brand didn’t offer a comparison with the Alphafly 4) and weighs 10% less in a men’s size 10. All that performance comes with an eye-watering price tag: This shoe will retail for $360 per pair.
Pros are already putting the Apex to work, and it has seen success—both the third place men’s and third place women’s finishers in the Chicago Marathon wore Apexes.

This is a milestone year for the New York City Marathon: Sunday’s race will be the 50th anniversary of the five-borough course, which was first run in 1976.
From its inaugural year in 1970, the race was held in Central Park. But five men—Ted Corbitt, Fred Lebow, George Spitz, Percy Sutton, and George Hirsch—spearheaded an effort to change the course to run through each of the city’s five boroughs, starting in Staten Island and ending in Manhattan.
Only one of the “trailblazers,” as the New York Road Runners calls them, is still alive. At 92, George Hirsch has seen the NYC Marathon develop from a fringe race in Central Park to the largest marathon in the world. A longtime magazine publisher (including at Runner’s World), Hirsch was the chairman of the NYRR board of directors from 2004 to 2023, and he helped generate the initial media buzz and funds for the 1976 race.
In an interview in mid-October, Hirsch shared his memories of the early days of the five-borough race and reflected on how it’s evolved over a half century.
A troubled city
The mid-1970s were a tough time to live in New York City. Crime was high, the economy was struggling, and thousands of residents fled for the suburbs. The city needed a pick-me-up, according to Hirsch. When Hirsch first heard the idea for a multi-borough race from Corbitt and Spitz, his immediate thought was that it would be a massive undertaking. Bridges would need to be closed, police hired, funds raised.
“Closing down a major city, the largest city in the United States, for a foot race was ambitious and it was unheard of at the time,” he said, noting that the Boston Marathon has a smaller footprint on the city proper. Still, the pioneers were able to secure the backing of the mayor, Abe Beame, although it was not pitched as a recurring event.
Now, they just needed to execute their idea. “Going into the [1976 race], our little running community was super excited about this New York Marathon,” Hirsch said. “But what we had no way of knowing was how the city was going to embrace it.”
So how did it go?
When Hirsch lined up on the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge in Staten Island in 1976, he was eager but a little nervous. That quickly changed, as he descended the bridge into Brooklyn.
“All of a sudden, there were crowds on both sides of the street yelling and cheering,” he remembered. “Sure, the crowds were nothing like they are today. Don’t misunderstand me. But by those days’ standards, it was extraordinary. And that was the way it was for our entire run.”
Hirsch ran 2:49:29 that day, placing 156th out of 1,539 finishers. Bill Rodgers won the men’s race, and Miki Gorman was the top woman. The atmosphere after the race was electric. Hirsch threw a party at his brownstone that night.
“It was clearly a victory party,” he said. “There was no question. It was a big celebration. We knew it had worked … It didn’t have to work. There’s a lot of things that can go wrong. And this one, it didn’t happen. It just worked. It was terrific, and we felt really great about it.”
The legacy of the marathon
After the success of the first year, the marathon began to steadily grow, and the five-borough format was adopted permanently. By 1980, there were 12,512 finishers. A decade later, there were 23,774. The race broke 40,000 finishers in 2009, and now it’s routinely one of the largest marathons in the world. Sunday’s race could see a record 60,000 participants.

Do you want a permanent income stream from the stocks you own? It's easy to find stocks with high dividend yields. Unfortunately, most of them are mature, sometimes stagnant businesses with only enough growth to support slow, steady increases.
Why not dial up the difficulty to find a generous dividend that can still easily outpace inflation for years to come? Philip Morris International (PM +2.67%) yields 3.2% and has raised its dividend annually since it began trading in 2008.
Its most recent increase, a hefty 8.8% bump, is impressive and no fluke. Here's why investors can buy, hold, and look forward to increasingly generous dividends from this tobacco giant for the foreseeable future.
The legacy business still shines
At first glance, it's fair to wonder why one might invest in tobacco stocks. Smoking rates have been declining for decades in the United States. However, Philip Morris primarily operates outside the United States, selling Marlboro worldwide.
The smoking decline isn't as straightforward in international markets, where rapid population growth has helped buoy the number of smokers despite the actual smoking rate decreasing.
Whereas sister company Altria Group, which sells Marlboro in America, reported a 3.2% decrease in domestic cigarette volume in the third quarter of 2026, Philip Morris' volumes held flat. Pricing power enabled the company to boost its organic gross profit from combustibles by 7.4%. In other words, cigarettes remain a very viable business internationally.
The future is coming sooner rather than later
That hasn't stopped Philip Morris from pushing to shift its business toward reduced-risk products, such as oral nicotine salt pouches, electronic vapes, and heat-not-burn tobacco devices.
The products have accounted for a whopping 42% of Philip Morris' net revenue through nine months of 2026. That puts Philip Morris squarely in the driver's seat in this industrywide race to a future beyond cigarettes.
With both major business segments thriving, Philip Morris has a strong growth outlook. Analysts see the company growing earnings by an average of nearly 9% annually over the next three to five years, and I wouldn't be shocked to see that pace sustained longer due to the immense pricing power nicotine creates.

We’ve all been there: You head out for an easy run and settle into your usual pace, but after a mile or two, your breathing feels labored and you notice your heart rate climbing higher than normal. However, you’re still going at your usual pace on your usual route, so what gives?
If you judge the run by pace alone, you might see no reason to change anything. But those other signals suggest you’re paying a higher price than usual to hold that speed.
Of course, you probably already know that factors like heat, hills, fatigue, and stress can make your usual pace feel harder. But with so much advice about what to pay attention to during a run, it can be tough to know which signals to trust and how to use them to evaluate your effort.
And without a clear way to interpret those signals, you might inadvertently push too hard on an easy day or miss the intended effort during a speed workout. Repeat these mistakes, and over time, you can disrupt the balance between training and recovery, making it harder to build the fitness you need to race your best.
The solution: A system from ultramarathon runner and endurance coach Nick Farr, head coach and founder of P3 Fitness. Farr organizes running feedback into three categories—performance output, biological load, and subjective feedback—and uses them together to understand how a run is unfolding.
Here’s how to use Farr’s three-category system to make every run count, build fitness more consistently, and arrive on race day ready to perform your best.
Why Your Run Data Needs Context
“No single metric tells you the whole story [of a run],” Farr says. For example, your pace tells you how fast you ran. But, inherently, it can’t tell you how difficult that pace felt or how your body responded to that pace.
To get a fuller picture, Farr separates training feedback into three categories, each of which answers one of those three questions:
- Performance output: What work are you doing?
- Biological load: How is your body responding to that work?
- Subjective feedback: How does the effort feel?
Evaluating the answers to these questions in concert with one another helps Farr and his athletes understand whether a run matches its intended purpose. It also gives runners a way to recognize when environmental conditions, fatigue, or other factors might call for an adjustment.
Performance Output: Shows What You’re Doing
Performance output describes the work you produce during a run. Metrics like pace, speed, distance, time, elevation, cadence, stride length, and power fall into this category, Farr says.
These metrics help you track what you accomplish. They show how quickly you covered a route, how far you ran, or how much climbing you tackled. You can also compare output across runs to see how your performance changes over time.
But output alone offers an incomplete view of the effort. You might finish an easy run at your usual pace, even though heat, hills, or fatigue made it much harder than normal. If you focus only on the pace number, you could miss the signs that you pushed beyond the effort you intended.
Biological Load: Reveals How Your Body Responds to Effort
Biological load, which Farr also calls internal or physiological load, describes how your body responds to the work you’re doing. Numbers such as heart rate, breathing rate, oxygen consumption, and core temperature can all offer information about your body’s response to a certain pace, environment, or training block.

Adobe (ADBE -0.66%) stock hit its closing record of $688.37 on Nov. 19, 2021. Almost five years later, shares of the creative software company trade around $248 as I write this -- about 64% off that high. And at their June 25 closing low of $193.41, they were down about 72%, the stock's deepest drop since the dot-com crash.
Deep drops are nothing new to Adobe, though. Using daily closing prices since 1990 (adjusted for stock splits, with dividends left out), the stock had fallen at least 30% from a record close eight times before this slide. It then set a new record after every one.
But I don't think that history settles much, because the two slumps this one most resembles started with a problem today's Adobe doesn't have.
Image source: Getty Images.
The slow comebacks took around six years
Six of the eight drops came in the 1990s, and they were deep, running from about 31% to 66%. But they were also mostly short.
Five of the six went from one record close to the next in around 18 months or less. The longest, which bottomed in August 1998, took about 3.4 years.
The two drops after that were another story. After peaking on Nov. 6, 2000, Adobe stock lost around 80% by August 2002, and it didn't close at a new record until Nov. 16, 2006.
The next slump, from an Oct. 24, 2007, peak, cut the stock around 67% by March 2009. Its next record was on July 12, 2013, about 5.7 years after the 2007 high.
Both times, the climb from the bottom back to the old high took over four years by itself. Today's slump is almost five years old, and as of this writing, the stock would have to gain around 177% to get back to its record.
In 2002 and 2009, the business shrank first
In the first of those long slumps, Adobe's revenue shrank two straight years, from fiscal 2000's $1.27 billion to $1.16 billion by fiscal 2002. Net income fell around a third over the same stretch.
Then sales turned. Revenue climbed 11% in fiscal 2003 and accelerated to 29% growth in fiscal 2004, so investors who hung on could see the rebound in the numbers.
The 2008-2009 recession cut deeper. Fiscal 2009 revenue slid 18%, to around $2.9 billion.
Interestingly, the stock's 2013 record was in a year when revenue fell 8%. Adobe had stopped new releases of its Creative Suite software, which customers bought outright, to focus on Creative Cloud subscriptions, which spread out revenue over time. Investors pushed the stock to a record before the new model's sales caught up.
Is this time different?
In one big way, it is: Adobe's business never shrank this time. Management expects fiscal 2026 revenue of around $26.6 billion, about 69% above the $15.8 billion it pulled in during fiscal 2021 -- the year the stock peaked.
Adobe's revenue climbed 13% year over year in its fiscal third quarter of 2026 (the period ending Aug. 28, 2026), hitting a quarterly record of $6.76 billion. Its non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share climbed even faster, up 15%.
The worry is what's next. Investors fear that artificial intelligence (AI) agents might take over tasks people now do with software like Adobe's, which bills subscribers per user, or seat.
If fewer people need a seat, Adobe's recurring revenue could shrink. That arguably makes this slump tougher to ride out than the past two. In 2002 and 2009, a sales recovery could show the hit was temporary. Now, Adobe needs to show that AI adds more to its business than it takes away.

Don't blame Intel's (INTC) weak guidance, tied to a prolonged memory chip supply shortage, for the fresh rout on tech stocks.
Blame the hyperscalers like Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL) and Meta (META) for not guiding Wall Street properly on how much they intended to spend this year and next on AI infrastructure. The bills are coming in much larger than expected, and Wall Street can't stomach it.
That's why you aren't seeing many heroes out there saying buy the dip right now. That's why Friday is shaping up to be another bloodbath for tech stocks.
Remember, it's cash flow that will be used to repay all the debt hyperscalers are poised to incur to support their robust AI infrastructure buildouts. The fact that cash flow is drying up because of a protracted period of spending is the bug causing the debt and stock markets to catch a cold.
Kudos to Amazon for at least not burying its free cash flow metric, the most important metric for tech at the moment, at the bottom of its earnings release. It made it no less tough to stomach, but at least it was easy to find quickly.
Amazon's free cash flow decreased to an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve months, driven primarily by a year-over-year increase of $94.8 billion in purchases of property and equipment. This increase primarily reflects investments in artificial intelligence, Amazon said.
This compares to a free cash flow inflow of $14.8 billion for the trailing twelve months ended Sept. 30 of last year.
"We still expect 2026 cash capex of approximately $220 billion, the majority for AWS, and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027," Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on his earnings call.
Amazon's stock is down 7% in pre-market trading today.

Thursday saw more than $500 billion in market value wiped off Google.

Editor’s Note: At our annual RW Shoe Summit meetings in New York City during the week leading up to the NYC Marathon, Adidas addressed durability concerns about the exposed section of forefoot foam. A small percentage of runners were seeing premature wear, so Adidas is going to extend the outsole material to better protect that section for all runners.
When Sabastian Sawe became the first official runner to break 2 hours in a marathon in an actual race, he was shod with Adidas’s latest $500 race rocket, the Adizero Adios Pro Evo 3. That shoe is incredibly fast, incredibly lightweight, and incredibly hard to get your hands on.
Today, Adidas released the next best thing: The Adizero Adios Pro 5. It’s the evolution of the brand’s best racing shoe, with learnings from the pricier Pro Evo 3. This time around, it’s lighter and uses a new carbon rim setup instead of rods. We got to test the shoe ahead of the announcement and have put it through some fast-paced workouts to see how it performs.
Can an Already Great Shoe Get Better?
Such is the nature of the beast that shoe companies must keep finding ways to change things up every 18 months or so. But, the Adios Pro 4 was an outstanding racer, so it didn’t really need a radical overhaul—just a nip here and tuck there. And it seems that’s mostly what Adidas did. It’s worth noting that we saw much the same situation with the recently announced Nike Alphafly 4. For that shoe, online commenters grumbled that it’s really just the Alphafly 3.1. But it had small tweaks that really improved on the formula. The same goes here.
The biggest improvement: weight. The Adios Pro has been on a diet the last few generations. My size 12 weighs just 7.3 oz, which is an ounce lighter than v4—and that shoe was a full ounce lighter than the previous model. The trimming puts the Adios Pro 5 right where it needs to be, on par with shoes like the Puma Fast-R 3, Asics MetaSpeed Sky/Edge, and Nike Vaporfly 4. There’s enough meat to the shoe to ensure long run support and durability, but no fat to slow it down.
The foam underfoot is Lightstrike Pro, but it feels ever-so-slightly firmer once you actually get running. I loved the underfoot feeling of the previous model—I could effortlessly jog a 20-miler or crank things up and run a sub-3 marathon. That’s rare versatility. The Pro 5 feels similarly suited; it has plenty of comfort, but has just a little more snap to it.
Straight out of the box, I took the shoe for a 9-mile jog and it felt just as cushy as any of my daily trainers. The next morning, I met up with a buddy, hanging on for dear life as he crushed 6 x 2K. I modified my run to 5 x 1 mile at 5:45 pace with a ¼ mile recovery and I still got dropped! But the shoe was a hit. I loved that I could feel the foam compress and load up with each footstrike, yet feel bouncy and responsive at toe off. These shoes wanted more than my legs could give.
Part of that comfy-yet-snappy sensation could be because Adidas filled in the gap under the arch and back half of the shoe. Previously, there was a window there that showed off the carbon rods, which also created a little wobble at mid-stance. With that extra foam making contact with the road, combined with the carbon rim (next section), the shoe seems better planted and stable as I work through my stride.
